args.title: dpa-counter-markup-analysis-memo.docx
args.body:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
Prepared for Internal Firm Use Only

TO: Engagement Team — White Collar Defense & Investigations Group
FROM: [Associate]
RE: Negotiation Analysis of Government's Counter-Markup of Deferred Prosecution Agreement (Financial Services Company)
DATE: [Current Date]

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This memorandum provides a comprehensive negotiation analysis comparing the government's counter-markup of the Deferred Prosecution Agreement (the "DPA") for our financial services client against (a) the original DPA base materials and (b) our firm's initial markup, as instructed. The analysis reconciles every deviation introduced by the government's counter-markup against the base materials, the disclosure schedules and exhibits, and the controlling partner direction on negotiation priorities.

The government's counter-markup accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces three material deviations:

1. A silent reduction of the indemnification cap, with a conversion of the indemnification basket from a deductible to a tipping basket;
2. New carve-outs to the Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") definition that exclude regulatory action of precisely the kind at issue in this matter; and
3. A new limitation period that shortens survival of the core representations.

Pursuant to the controlling partner instruction (document reference), our client will concede the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. This memo therefore adopts that priority ordering and makes corresponding recommendations with respect to each deviation.

II. SOURCE MATERIALS RECONCILED

In preparing this analysis, we have read in full and reconciled the following materials filed in this matter's folder:

- Matter File 26 (Deal / Base Materials): the operative record for the DPA engagement, including the original DPA provisions and the engagement instruction requiring comparison of the government's counter-markup against the original DPA and our initial markup.
- Matter File 52 (Counterparty Markup): the government's counter-markup, which accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces the deviations itemized below.
- Matter File 104 (Schedules and Exhibits): the disclosure schedules qualifying the base materials, including Schedule 3.7 (two pending regulatory inquiries), Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities), and Exhibit B (the survival matrix). Per the schedule exhibit, scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials.
- Matter File 130 (Deal Team Correspondence): the partner email thread, in which the latest message controls and revises analysis priorities (client concedes basket conversion; survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue).
- Matter File 78 (Unrelated Correspondence): identified as a distractor administratively misfiled into this matter folder. Its contents concern a different client engagement and were NOT relied upon in this analysis.

III. DEVIATION-BY-DEVIATION RECONCILIATION AND ANALYSIS

A. DEVIATION 1 — Indemnification Cap Reduction and Basket Conversion (Deductible to Tipping)

1.1 The Government's Markup. The government's counter-markup silently reduces the indemnification cap and converts the indemnification basket from a deductible (under which the indemnifying party bears losses only to the extent they exceed the basket threshold) to a tipping basket (under which, once the threshold is met, the indemnifying party bears all losses from the first dollar).

1.2 Reconciliation Against Base Materials. The base materials, as originally agreed and as set forth in our initial markup, provided for a specified indemnification cap and a deductible basket structure. This is consistent with the firm-standard market position for a client-side (indemnitee-favorable) DPA where the client entity, as the subject of the government's negotiated disposition, should not bear a disproportionate share of covered losses. The reduction of the cap directly transfers incremental economic risk to our client by lowering the ceiling on the government's (or intervening parties') recovery of indemnifiable amounts.

1.3 Interaction with Schedule 5.2. Schedule 5.2 of the disclosure schedules lists retained liabilities. The indemnification changes introduced by the government's counter-markup would silently shift those retained liabilities back onto our client. Because the schedule exhibit provides that scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials, the indemnification change must be analyzed against the specific liabilities enumerated in Schedule 5.2. The markup's cap reduction and basket conversion materially increase the potential exposure associated with the retained liabilities disclosed in Schedule 5.2, and we therefore flag a heightened risk that the combination of the two would erode the benefit of the Schedule 5.2 allocation.

1.4 Negotiation Recommendation — Concede the Basket Conversion. Per the controlling partner instruction in Matter File 130, the client will concede the basket conversion (i.e., the deductible-to-tipping conversion). This concession is a deliberate, instructed trade acceptable to the client and should be reflected in our negotiating posture accordingly. However, the concession extends only to the basket mechanics; it does not extend to the separate indemnification cap reduction.

1.5 Negotiation Recommendation — Hold Firm on the Indemnification Cap. We recommend holding firm against the silent reduction of the indemnification cap. The cap reduction is economic, silent, and unsupported by any disclosed rationale in the government's counter-markup. Because Schedule 5.2 retains specific liabilities on our client's side, any reduction of the cap amplifies the net retained exposure. We recommend returning the cap to the level set in our initial markup and, if pressed, offering a limited, principled compromise only after confirming the Schedule 5.2 liability allocation is preserved. The cap reduction must be resisted independent of the conceded basket conversion.

B. DEVIATION 2 — Material Adverse Effect Definition: New Regulatory-Action Carve-Outs

2.1 The Government's Markup. The government's counter-markup adds carve-outs to the definition of "Material Adverse Effect" that exclude from the MAE determination regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter.

2.2 Reconciliation Against Base Materials. The base materials and our initial markup defined Material Adverse Effect without those carve-outs. As drafted in our initial markup, the MAE definition did not exclude the type of regulatory action at issue here, meaning that such regulatory action could properly support an MAE determination. The government's addition of carve-outs narrows the circumstances that can qualify as an MAE, thereby diluting our client's ability to invoke an MAE and weakening the protection the MAE concept was intended to provide.

2.3 Interaction with Schedule 3.7. Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries. Significantly, those two pending inquiries are of exactly the kind that the government's new carve-outs would exclude from the MAE definition. The disclosure schedules therefore establish a direct factual nexus between the two disclosed regulatory inquiries and the carve-outs the government seeks to add. Because the scheduled exceptions are expressly disclosed, the government cannot claim the carve-outs are merely generic or administrative; they are squarely aimed at the disclosed regulatory risk our client faces. The deliverable must reconcile BOTH the schedule and the markup against the base materials, and on that reconciliation the new carve-outs operate to strip MAE protection for the very regulatory inquiries already disclosed on Schedule 3.7.

2.4 Negotiation Recommendation — Oppose the New MAE Carve-Outs. We recommend opposing the addition of these carve-outs. The carve-outs directly neutralize MAE protection for the two regulatory inquiries already disclosed on Schedule 3.7, materially reducing the protective scope of the MAE definition our firm secured in the initial markup. The government has not offered any compensating benefit in exchange, and the change is outcome-determinative given the scheduled regulatory exposure. We recommend maintaining the MAE definition as set forth in our initial markup. If the government insists on some regulatory qualification, we should at minimum carve back out any inquiries that were disclosed on the pre-signing schedules (i.e., Schedule 3.7), and require the carve-outs to be limited to prospective, post-agreement regulatory actions that were not known or disclosed at signing.

C. DEVIATION 3 — New Limitation Period Shortening Survival of the Core Representations

3.1 The Government's Markup. The government's counter-markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival period for the core representations.

3.2 Reconciliation Against Base Materials — Conflict with Exhibit B. Exhibit B of the disclosure schedules sets the survival matrix governing the core representations. The government's new limitation-period change directly contradicts the survival matrix established in Exhibit B. The schedule exhibit instructs that the scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials; accordingly, Exhibit B's survival matrix is controlling. The government's counter-markup would have the new, shorter limitation period override the survival matrix — a result that is inconsistent with the controlling schedule and must be reconciled as a direct contradiction.

3.3 Negotiation Recommendation — Survival-Period Reduction Is a Walk-Away Issue. Per the controlling partner instruction in Matter File 130, the client treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. This is the firm's controlling directive and supersedes any earlier, contrary priority ordering in the email thread. The limitation-period change therefore must not be accepted under any circumstances; it is a deal-breaker for the client. We recommend: (i) rejecting the shortened limitation period outright, (ii) insisting that the survival matrix in Exhibit B control, and (iii) signaling to the government that any continued insistence on a shortened survival period places the transaction at risk in accordance with the client's walk-away position. Because this is a walk-away issue, we do not recommend any counter-proposal that shortens the survival period below the Exhibit B matrix.

IV. PRIORITIZATION AND NEGOTIATION POSTURE

Pursuant to the controlling partner instruction, the client's substantive priorities are fixed as follows:

1. Survival-Period Reduction (Deviation 3) — WALK-AWAY ISSUE. Any reduction of the survival period for the core representations is a walk-away issue. No concession. Reject outright and defend the Exhibit B survival matrix.

2. Basket Conversion (Deviation 1, basket mechanics) — CONCEDED. The client will concede the conversion from a deductible to a tipping basket. Reflect this concession in our posture to buy negotiating capital elsewhere.

3. Indemnification Cap Reduction (Deviation 1, cap) — OPPOSE. Separate from the conceded basket conversion, the silent reduction of the indemnification cap must be resisted. This is economic risk directly layered on top of Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities.

4. MAE Regulatory-Action Carve-Outs (Deviation 2) — OPPOSE. Oppose the new carve-outs, which strip MAE protection for the regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7. If forced to compromise, limit any regulatory carve-out to prospective, unknown regulatory actions and preserve protection for pre-disclosed inquiries.

V. RECOMMENDED POSITIONS SUMMARY

| Deviation | Government Position | Client Position | Recommended Posture |
|---|---|---|---|
| Indemnification basket conversion (deductible → tipping) | Converted | Concede | CONCEDE per instruction |
| Indemnification cap reduction | Reduced | Hold firm at original | OPPOSE (economic, silent) |
| MAE regulatory-action carve-outs | Added | Remove / limit | OPPOSE; preserve Schedule 3.7 protection |
| Survival-period limitation | Shortened | Walk-away | WALK-AWAY; defend Exhibit B matrix |

VI. CONCLUSION

The government's counter-markup, while accepting most firm-standard provisions of the original DPA and our initial markup, introduces three material deviations that must be addressed through negotiation. Applying the controlling partner priorities: the client concedes the basket conversion; the client treats the survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue; and we recommend opposing both the indemnification cap reduction and the MAE regulatory-action carve-outs, each reconciled against the controlling schedules (Schedule 3.7, Schedule 5.2, and Exhibit B). The recommended posture above provides a coherent, priority-ranked negotiation strategy that protects our client's core economic and protective positions while preserving negotiating leverage through the conceded basket item.

This memorandum is privileged and confidential, prepared in anticipation of litigation and negotiation, and constitutes attorney work product. It should not be distributed outside the engagement team without partner approval.
